response.passage: Rohan is designing a rectangular garden game board where the area must be exactly 40 square units. He writes the equation x² - 3x = 40 to represent the dimensions. To solve this, he first rearranges it into the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, identifying a=1, b=-3, and c=-40. Rohan knows that for any quadratic equation, the discriminant D = b² - 4ac helps determine the nature of the roots. He calculates D = (-3)² - 4(1)(-40), which equals 9 + 160 = 169. Since 169 is greater than zero, he concludes there are two distinct real roots. He then factors the equation into (x - 8)(x + 5) = 0. He realizes that while x = 8 and x = -5 are both mathematical solutions to the equation, a physical length cannot be negative. Therefore, he rejects x = -5 and keeps x = 8 as the only valid dimension for his garden board. He checks his work by substituting 8 back into the original expression, confirming that 8² - 3(8) indeed equals 40. Rohan successfully avoids common traps, ensuring his quadratic model perfectly matches the physical reality of his game design.
response.summary: Rohan models a garden board area using a quadratic equation and solves it systematically. He correctly identifies the standard form and uses the discriminant to understand the roots. Finally, he validates his solution by rejecting physically impossible values.
